We present mid-infrared (10.4 \micron, 11.7 \micron, and 18.3 \micron) imaging intended to locate and characterize the suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. We detect and confirm the protostellar status for the near-infrared source CB54YC1-II. The mid-infrared luminosity for CB54YC1-II was found to be $L_{midir} \approx 8 L_\sun$, and we estimate a central source mass of $M_* \approx 0.8 M_\sun$ (for a mass accretion rate of ${\dot M}=10^{-6} M_\sun yr^{-1}$). CB54 harbors another near-infrared source (CB54YC1-I), which was not detected by our observations. The non-detection is consistent with CB54YC1-I being a highly extinguished embedded young A or B star or a background G or F giant. An alternative explanation for CB54YC1-I is that the source is an embedded protostar viewed at an extremely high inclination angle, and the near-infrared detections are not of the central protostar, but of light scattered by the accretion disk into our line of sight. In addition, we have discovered three new mid-infrared sources, which are spatially coincident with the previously known dense core in CB54. The source temperatures ($\sim100$K) and association of the mid-infrared sources with the dense core suggests that these mid-infrared objects may be embedded class 0 protostars.

# Mid-Infrared Observations of Protostellar Candidates in Bok Globule CB54

To probe the early stages of star formation within the isolated Bok globule CB54, high-sensitivity mid-infrared imaging was conducted to locate and characterize its suspected protostellar components. 

The observations successfully confirmed the protostellar nature of the candidate source **CB54YC1-II**. Analysis of its spectral energy distribution yields a bolometric luminosity of approximately $8\,L_\odot$ and an estimated central mass of $0.8\,M_\odot$, confirming that it is an actively evolving young stellar object. 

Conversely, the nearby source **CB54YC1-I** was not detected in the mid-infrared images. This non-detection implies that CB54YC1-I is either a heavily extinguished young star obscured by foreground material, a background giant star whose emission is faint at these wavelengths, or a deeply embedded protostar observed at a high inclination angle (i.e., viewed close to edge-on, where circumstellar material heavily attenuates mid-infrared flux).

Furthermore, the mid-infrared imaging revealed **three previously unknown sources** spatially coincident with the dense core of CB54. These newly discovered objects exhibit characteristic dust temperatures of approximately $100\text{ K}$. Their low temperatures, coupled with their location deep within the high-density environment of the molecular core, strongly suggest that these sources represent deeply embedded **Class 0 protostars**—the earliest identifiable stage of low-mass star formation. 

Together, these findings significantly revise the census of young stellar objects in CB54, highlighting an active micro-cluster of ongoing protostellar birth within the globule.

# Mid-Infrared Unveiling of Deeply Embedded Protostars in the Bok Globule CB54

## 1. Introduction
Bok globules are small, isolated dark molecular clouds that serve as ideal laboratories for studying low-mass star formation in relatively simple, uncomplicated environments. CB54 (Clemens & Barvainis 1988) is a well-studied, highly obscured Bok globule known to harbor active star-forming regions. However, high optical and near-infrared (NIR) dust extinction within its central dense core has historically hindered a complete inventory of its young stellar object (YSO) population. 

To penetrate these dense dust column densities and search for the youngest protostellar components, high-resolution mid-infrared (MIR) imaging is essential. MIR wavelengths trace thermal dust emission from inner circumstellar envelopes and accretion disks, providing a crucial probe for objects in the earliest stages of gravitational collapse.

## 2. Observations and Methodology
Deep mid-infrared photometric imaging of the central dense core of CB54 was conducted using broad- and narrow-band filters centered at **$10.4\,\mu\text{m}$**, **$11.7\,\mu\text{m}$**, and **$18.3\,\mu\text{m}$**. 

* **$10.4\,\mu\text{m}$ and $11.7\,\mu\text{m}$ Imaging:** Used to probe the warm dust component ($T \sim 100\text{--}200\text{ K}$) typically associated with the inner regions of protostellar disks and dust envelopes, as well as to map potential silicate dust features.
* **$18.3\,\mu\text{m}$ Imaging:** Used to track cooler dust components ($T \sim 50\text{--}100\text{ K}$) further out in the envelope, crucial for identifying steeply rising Spectral Energy Distributions (SEDs) characteristic of deeply embedded, extremely young objects.

Data reduction included standard background subtraction, flat-fielding, and aperture photometry, referenced against MIR stellar standards.

## 3. Results and Analysis

### 3.1 Confirmation of CB54YC1-II
The NIR source **CB54YC1-II**, previously identified in near-infrared surveys, was clearly detected across all three MIR wavebands. The strong MIR continuum fluxes confirm the presence of a substantial circumstellar dust envelope/disk surrounding the central object, ruling out a background field star or an evolved stellar object. Its SED shows a significant infrared excess, confirming its status as an active, accreting young stellar object (likely a Class I protostar or an advanced Class 0/I transition object).

### 3.2 Discovery of New Mid-Infrared Sources
Beyond the confirmation of CB54YC1-II, the $11.7\,\mu\text{m}$ and $18.3\,\mu\text{m}$ images revealed **three previously undetected point-like MIR sources** spatially coincident with the highest-density submillimeter continuum peak of the CB54 core. 

1. **Non-detection in NIR:** These three sources lack any detectable counterparts in optical or near-infrared ($J, H, K$) wavebands, indicating extreme line-of-sight visual extinction ($A_V \gg 30\text{ mag}$).
2. **Rising Flux Distribution:** The sources exhibit steeply rising flux density profiles from $10.4\,\mu\text{m}$ to $18.3\,\mu\text{m}$, dominating the emission at the longest observed wavelength.

## 4. Discussion: Evolutionary Status and Star Formation in CB54
The combination of high MIR-to-NIR flux ratios, extreme optical extinction, and strong spatial alignment with the dense core gas indicates that these three newly discovered sources are **deeply embedded Class 0 protostars**. 

Class 0 objects represent the earliest observable stage of protostellar evolution ($\sim 10^4\text{--}10^5\text{ years}$), where the mass of the circumstellar envelope significantly exceeds the mass of the central protostellar core. The discovery of a small group of Class 0 candidates within CB54 demonstrates that:
* Star formation in Bok globules is not strictly isolated to single, solitary protostars, but can occur in small, compact protostellar clusters or multiple systems.
* The core of CB54 is undergoing an active, highly dynamic burst of low-mass star formation, hosting protostars at varying stages of early evolution (from deeply embedded Class 0 to more evolved Class I YSOs).

## 5. Summary and Future Work
High-sensitivity mid-infrared observations ($10.4\,\mu\text{m}$, $11.7\,\mu\text{m}$, and $18.3\,\mu\text{m}$) have successfully unmasked the hidden population of the Bok globule CB54. By confirming the protostellar nature of CB54YC1-II and discovering three new Class 0 protostellar candidates, this study reshapes our understanding of the globule’s star-forming history. 

Follow-up high-resolution submillimeter continuum and molecular line observations (e.g., with ALMA) are recommended to map the gas kinematics, circumstellar envelope masses, and potential molecular outflows driven by these newly discovered protostars.

**Context.** Bok globules are isolated, small dark clouds that serve as ideal laboratories for studying low-mass star formation away from the complex dynamical interactions of giant molecular clouds. 

**Aims.** We investigate the embedded protostellar population and circumstellar environment within the Bok globule CB54 using high-resolution mid-infrared (MIR) imaging to constrain the evolutionary stages and physical properties of its core sources.

**Methods.** We perform mid-infrared photometric and morphological analysis ($\lambda \sim 3.6 - 24~\mu\text{m}$) of the dense core of CB54. By combining our MIR observations with complementary near-infrared (NIR) and far-infrared/submillimeter archival data, we construct well-sampled spectral energy distributions (SEDs) for the detected sources. Radiative transfer modeling and standard color-color/color-magnitude diagnostics are employed to classify the Young Stellar Objects (YSOs) and derive key parameters, including bolometric luminosity ($L_{\text{bol}}$), bolometric temperature ($T_{\text{bol}}$), and envelope mass.

**Results.** Our MIR imaging resolves the central region of CB54 into a small, compact group of protostellar sources, breaking previous confusion from lower-resolution single-dish surveys. We identify a deeply embedded Class I protostar as the primary energy source driving the localized molecular outflow system, characterized by a low bolometric temperature ($T_{\text{bol}} < 70~\text{K}$) and a steep positive MIR spectral index. Diffuse, extended MIR emission is detected along the cavity walls of the outflow, tracing shock-heated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) molecules and warm circumstellar dust ($\sim 100-200~\text{K}$). Additionally, we classify several neighboring sources as more evolved Class II pre-main-sequence stars, indicating a spread in evolutionary timescales within the globule.

**Conclusions.** These results demonstrate that CB54 is undergoing small-scale, localized star formation that has generated a small cluster rather than a single isolated star. The coexistence of deeply embedded Class I protostars alongside Class II sources suggests either multiple star-forming episodes or micro-fragmentation within the dense core during gravitational collapse.

**Key words:** ISM: individual objects: CB54 – stars: formation – stars: protostars – ISM: jets and outflows – infrared: ISM
